## Stakes (Extrapolating) {#intro}

**Not in the LLGA 2026–2027 list.** In 2026–2027 the Period 2 management units of the track are **IME_52441_EP — Simulation d’entreprise**, a one-day serious game in which teams of five run competing multinational phone makers (R&D, plant sizing, pricing, accounting, responsible-sourcing trade-offs), and **IME_52470_EP — Digital Transformation and AI in Organisations and Society** (Daniel Curto), on how AI systems reshape organisations, work and decision-making once they leave the lab (group project and individual exam).

The startup/entrepreneurship pair below comes from the earlier wiki curriculum and is kept as background. Extrapolated notes. Brochure title: **Startup and Large Companies: Building a Bridge for Innovation** *or* **Entrepreneurship for Sustainability / Case Studies on Innovation**. Shared thread: how an innovation (often technical) crosses the startup ↔ large-company boundary under governance, risk, and sometimes sustainability constraints.

In the wiki curriculum, the pair followed P1 strategy/marketing with cases: alliances, scaling, and friction between startup speed and corporate process — very visible when industrializing an AI model. The official case material is not reproduced here; [one illustrative case](#case) shows the reasoning on a Period 2 demo.

## Place in the 2-year path {#place}

**Upstream**: [Strategy / Marketing](../m1p1-strategy-marketing/index.html). **Here (P2 in the wiki curriculum)**: applied innovation during the RL / Graph ML / NLP core; in 2026–2027 the Period 2 management slot is held by IME_52441_EP and IME_52470_EP. **Downstream**: P3 [research internship](../m1p3-research-internship/index.html), then M2 [transverse project](../m2-projet-transverse/index.html) + [final internship](../m2-internship/index.html).

## Industry and research links {#industrie}

**Industry**: intrapreneurship, corporate venture, tech transfer, AI product ops. **Research**: result maturity (TRL), IP, open-source vs proprietary — recurring in lab internships and CIFRE.

## A worked case: the graph+text demo {#case}

[Illustrative]{.tag} An invented scenario, with no real company behind it. It applies the bridge questions of [How to approach it](#travailler) to one Period 2 deliverable.

**The demo.** A student team has built the question-answering system of capstone [Y1.1](../../projects/index.html#y1-1): text becomes a knowledge graph (NLP), a retriever walks the graph (Graph ML), a bandit learns which retrieval mode is worth its token cost (RL), and an LLM writes the answer with its sources. A mid-size industrial company wants it for its maintenance manuals. One team member would rather found a startup around it.

**Step 1 — Who pays, who uses, who operates.**

-   The payer is the head of maintenance, who owns the budget and must see fewer hours lost searching manuals.
-   The users are about 300 technicians, often on a tablet in a workshop.
-   The operator is the company's IT team on the corporate route, or the startup on the spin-off route. Whoever operates also answers the call when an answer is wrong.

**Step 2 — Maturity.** On the technology readiness level (TRL) scale, the demo is at TRL 4: validated in the lab, on a public proxy corpus. Run on the company's own manuals, it reaches TRL 5–6 (validated, then demonstrated, in a relevant environment). A pilot used by technicians in the workshop is TRL 7. The gap is work the demo skipped: per-document access rights, refreshing the graph when a manual changes, and a test set written with technicians.

**Step 3 — Risk register.**

-   *Data*: confidential manuals leave the company network if the LLM is a remote API. Mitigation: a contract with no data retention, or a self-hosted open-weights model.
-   *Wrong answers*: an invented torque value can damage a machine. Mitigation: answer only from a cited passage, and abstain otherwise.
-   *Dependency*: the whole product rests on one model provider and one licence. Mitigation: keep a second model that passes the same tests, and check that the model licence allows commercial use.

**Step 4 — Two routes.**

|                      | Spin-off startup                                         | Corporate pilot (intrapreneurship)              |
|----------------------|----------------------------------------------------------|-------------------------------------------------|
| Speed                | Weeks to a first pilot                                   | Months: purchasing, security review, legal      |
| Money                | Founders' time, grants, then a seed round                | An internal budget and a sponsoring manager     |
| Who owns the IP      | The startup, under a licence from the school or lab if needed | The company, as the contract says          |
| Main risk            | One customer and no second source of revenue             | The pilot never leaves the innovation lab       |
| Success looks like   | A second paying customer                                 | The system enters the IT run budget             |

**Step 5 — Cost check.** Take requests the size of the worked example in [MLOps ch. 4](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html#ch4), a Year 2 course: 1,500 tokens in and 300 out, at its illustrative API prices.

-   Volume: 300 technicians × 10 questions per working day × 20 working days give about 60,000 requests a month.
-   API bill: 0.0027 € per request, so 60,000 × 0.0027 € ≈ 160 € a month.
-   Own model: that example's break-even volumes are about 185,000 requests a month (distilled 1B student) and 580,000 (fine-tuned 8B), three to ten times this volume.
-   Verdict: price favours the API. A case for self-hosting has to come from the data constraint of Step 3.

**What the case teaches.** The model was the easy part. The bridge is decided by who signs the run budget after the pilot, who answers for a wrong answer, and whether the data may leave the building.

## How to approach it {#travailler}

-   Take a P2 technical deliverable (e.g. the graph+text demo of capstone [Y1.1](../../projects/index.html#y1-1) or [Y1.3](../../projects/index.html#y1-3)) and write the startup/corporate “bridge”: who pays, who operates, what risk. The [worked case](#case) shows the five steps.
-   For the cost argument, compute the cost per request and the break-even volume between an API and your own model with [MLOps ch. 4](../m2-mlops-llm-engineering/index.html#ch4) (Year 2; Proposition 4.2 gives the break-even volume).
-   If the sustainability option is chosen, cross-link with [Optimization for AI](../m1p2-optimization-ai/index.html) (APM_52067_EP, Period 2; [ch. 10](../m1p2-optimization-ai/index.html#ch10) on training networks) and [Optimization and Responsible AI for Sustainability](../m1p2-responsible-ai-sustainability/index.html), whose [ch. 6](../m1p2-responsible-ai-sustainability/index.html#ch6) measures the energy and carbon footprint and whose [ch. 3](../m1p2-responsible-ai-sustainability/index.html#ch3) gives the frugality levers.
-   The responsible-AI module is no longer a Period 2 companion: in 2026–2027 it is taught in Period 1 as CSC_51076_EP and is not in the LLGA lists.

[Extrapolating]{.tag} Framing support; the case above is illustrative, and official cases and grading belong to the course units actually taught (in 2026–2027, IME_52441_EP and IME_52470_EP).
